modules.d: Build software by describing it in plain language — what 'vibe coding' really is, and what it isn't.
modules.body:
You can now build software without learning to code

For decades, turning an idea into working software meant years of learning syntax, frameworks, and tooling. That wall just came down. Vibe coding — a term popularized in 2025 — means building applications by describing what you want in plain language and letting AI write, run, and fix the code. You direct; the AI implements. This course takes you from idea to a live app on a real phone, and then to income — no computer-science degree required.

"The hottest new programming language is English." — Andrej Karpathy, who coined the phrase that captured the shift. You already speak the language of the AI age; vibe coding is where speaking it precisely becomes building.

What vibe coding actually is

  • You describe, AI builds. "Make an app where users log their daily water intake and see a weekly chart" — the AI generates the working code.
  • You iterate in conversation. "Make the button bigger, add a dark mode, save data between sessions" — you refine by talking, not typing syntax.
  • You test and direct, the AI implements. Your job is vision, judgment, and taste; the AI handles the mechanics.

What vibe coding is NOT (the honest boundaries)

  • Not magic — it's a skill. The quality of what you build tracks the clarity of how you direct. Vague prompts make broken apps; precise ones make real products. That's what this course trains.
  • Not a replacement for understanding. You don't need to write code, but you do need to understand what your app should do, how users move through it, and when something's wrong. Judgment doesn't get automated.
  • Not (yet) for safety-critical systems. Great for tools, prototypes, MVPs, personal and business apps. For medical devices, banking cores, or anything where a bug endangers people, human engineers still own the work — Commandment 3.
The mindset flip: stop thinking "I can't code, so I can't build." Start thinking "I can describe what I want clearly, so I can build." The bottleneck is no longer syntax — it's the clarity of your thinking. Everything in Level 1 (CLEAR prompting) and Level 2 (operating systems) pays off here.

The tools you'll use

AI app builders that turn descriptions into live apps — platforms like Lovable, Bolt, v0, Replit, and Cursor — plus the reasoning models (Claude, GPT) you already know for planning and debugging. Tools change fast, so this course teaches the method, which outlasts any specific product. You'll verify current features as you go.

🧪 Validated exercise

In vibe coding, the new bottleneck is no longer syntax — it's the ___ of your thinking.

🔬 Going deeper: what actually happens when you "vibe"

When you describe an app, the builder's language model writes real code: a front end (the screens users see, usually HTML, CSS and a JavaScript framework such as React), often a back end (logic that runs on a server), and a database (where information is stored). The model predicts code that matches your description and the patterns it learned from millions of projects. That is why clarity matters so much: an ambiguous request ("make it nice") forces the model to guess, while a precise one ("a list of today's sales, newest first, each showing item, price and profit") leaves little to guess.

Two practical consequences follow. First, the model has a limited context window — over a long session it can lose track of earlier decisions, so keep a written spec and prompt log you can paste back in. Second, generated code can contain mistakes and security weaknesses even when the app appears to work. You do not need to read every line, but you must test behaviour carefully and follow basic safety rules: never paste passwords or secret keys into your app's visible code, and treat any app that stores other people's data with extra care (Module 8).

Your role is that of a product owner and quality inspector: you decide what should exist, describe it precisely, and judge whether what was built is right. That judgement — not syntax — is the scarce skill.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Clarity is the whole game. Before you build, be able to say in one sentence what your app does and for whom.
  • Learn the method, not the tool. App builders change monthly; the way you plan, prompt, and debug carries across all of them.
  • Start small and real. Your first app should solve one genuine problem for one real person — ideally you.

📚 Glossary

  • Vibe coding: building software by describing it in natural language, with AI writing the code.
  • MVP: minimum viable product — the smallest working version.
  • App builder: an AI platform that turns descriptions into live apps.
  • Iteration: refining an app through successive conversational changes.

📖 Explore further

  • Tools to explore (verify current features): Lovable · Bolt · Replit.
  • This course builds directly on Level 1 CLEAR prompting and Level 2 operator systems.

quiz.q: Amina, a nurse in Garoua, wants to vibe-code an app that calculates insulin doses and sends commands directly to patients' insulin pumps. Based on the module's boundaries, what is the soundest advice?
opts: Build it with a top AI builder, then test it thoroughly on herself and colleagues before release
Use vibe coding for a prototype of the idea, but leave the dosing system to engineers
Write the prompts with extra precision so the AI produces medically safe code
Build it, but add a disclaimer that users are responsible for checking every dose
quiz.x: Safety-critical systems such as dosing stay with human engineers; vibe coding suits a prototype to explore the idea. Extra-precise prompts help quality but do not make a bug-endangers-people system acceptable.

quiz.q: A Lagos shop owner says: 'Since I can't write code, I'll let the AI decide what the app should do and just accept whatever it builds.' Which correction best reflects the module?
opts: Partly right: she should accept the code but ask the AI to choose a nicer colour scheme
She should first learn basic JavaScript so she can check each line the AI writes
She keeps the product-owner role: deciding what should exist and judging what was built
Correct: the AI handles both the vision and the mechanics, so accepting its output is efficient
quiz.x: Your role is product owner: vision, judgement and testing behaviour. Learning JavaScript is the runner-up but misses the point that you don't need syntax, you need judgement.

quiz.q: Two learners build the same water-tracker. Kofi prompts 'make a nice water app'; Ruth prompts 'one screen, a +1 glass button, a daily goal of 8, and a 7-day bar chart'. What does the module predict?
opts: Ruth's app will be closer to what's needed, because output tracks prompt clarity
Kofi gets the better app, because vague prompts leave the AI room to be creative
Ruth gets the better app, provided she also writes some of the chart code herself and checks it
Both get similar apps, because modern builders fill in missing detail reliably
quiz.x: Quality tracks the clarity of direction; vague prompts make broken apps. Builders do fill gaps, but with guesses, so 'similar apps' is the tempting yet wrong runner-up.

quiz.q: A US church volunteer builds a member-directory app and pastes the database admin password directly into the page code 'so it connects faster'. What is the main problem the module highlights?
opts: The password should be shortened so it is harder for visitors to notice in the code
The app will load slower because passwords add weight to the page code and every request
Nothing serious, as long as the app is shared with the church's members and no one else
Anyone viewing the page source could read the secret; keys belong in secret settings
quiz.x: Never put passwords or API keys in visible code; they belong in server-side or platform secret settings. Limiting sharing to members is the runner-up, but links spread and source is still readable.

quiz.q: A Douala student asks which three layers an AI builder generates when she describes a booking app. Which mapping of her app's parts to layers is correct?
opts: Booking form = front end; slots logic = back end; stored bookings = database
Booking form = front end; slots logic = database; stored bookings = back end
Booking form = database; available slots logic = front end; stored bookings = back end
Booking form = back end; slots logic = database; stored bookings = front end
quiz.x: Screens users see are the front end, logic runs on the back end, and data is kept in the database. The last option is the runner-up: it gets the form right but swaps logic and storage.

quiz.q: Pierre runs a small Yaoundé clinic and wants a booking app that stores patients' phone numbers. Using the module's 'good fit or not' sorting, how should he treat this project?
opts: A fit as long as he keeps the app offline and does not deploy it to a live link
Unsuitable: any app with personal data has to be left to experienced engineers
A great fit with no special steps, since a booking app is a simple tool
A fit with extra care: add security checks because it holds real users' data
quiz.x: Apps holding others' personal data are a fit with extra care. Calling it a plain great fit is the runner-up but skips the security checks real users' data demands.

quiz.q: A mentor tells a Kumba cohort: 'The bottleneck is no longer syntax.' A learner asks what the bottleneck now is. Which answer matches the module?
opts: Access to the most expensive AI builder subscriptions and the fastest laptop available
Memorising the names of frameworks such as React so the AI can be steered
The clarity of your thinking about what to build and how users move through it

quiz.x: The mindset flip: clarity of thinking is the new bottleneck. Knowing framework names can help steer, which makes it the runner-up, but it is not what limits most builders.

quiz.q: Which statement about the origin of the term 'vibe coding' is accurate according to the module's facts?
opts: It was coined by Steve Jobs when describing how Apple shipped the first iPhone apps
It was coined by Andrej Karpathy in a post on X in February 2025, and spread quickly
It was introduced by Fred Brooks in The Mythical Man-Month to describe fast building
It was coined by Grace Hopper's team in 1947 to describe their debugging by conversation
quiz.x: Karpathy coined the phrase in February 2025 on X. The other names come from other module facts (the 1947 moth, Brooks's law, 'Real artists ship'), which is what makes them tempting.

quiz.q: A Bamenda teacher's vibe-coded flashcard app works, but she cannot tell when a card shows the wrong answer because she never defined what correct behaviour looks like. Which 'not' boundary does this illustrate?
opts: Vibe coding is not for safety-critical systems such as banking cores

It does not replace understanding what the app should do and spotting errors
Vibe coding is not free, because every AI builder charges a fee per prompt
quiz.x: It is not a replacement for understanding: you must know what the app should do and notice when it's wrong. 'Not magic' is the runner-up, but a longer prompt won't help if she can't judge the output.

modules.d: Before you build anything, define who it's for and what problem it kills — the blueprint stage.
modules.body:
The step everyone skips — and why it wrecks their app

The most common vibe-coding failure isn't bad code; it's building the wrong thing beautifully. Before you touch an app builder, you map three things: the idea, the user, and the problem. This blueprint is what turns "an app" into "an app someone actually wants." Ten minutes here saves ten hours of rebuilding.

The three questions that define your app

  • Who exactly is the user? Not "everyone." A specific person: "market vendors in Yaoundé who track daily sales on paper." The narrower the user, the clearer the app.
  • What painful problem does it solve? The app must remove a real friction: "they lose track of which goods sell and can't see profit." No pain, no app.
  • What's the one core action? The single thing a user does that delivers the value: "log a sale in two taps and see today's profit." Everything else is secondary.
"Fall in love with the problem, not the solution." — a startup maxim that's doubly true for builders. The app is just today's answer to the problem; the problem is what keeps users coming back. Map it before you build.

From problem to feature list (with AI's help)

Once the problem is clear, AI helps you translate it into a lean feature set:

  1. Core feature: the one action that delivers the value. Build this first, alone.
  2. Supporting features: the few things that make the core usable (e.g. save data, see history).
  3. Later features: everything nice-to-have goes on a "not yet" list. Ruthlessly defer.
The one-sentence app spec: "[App name] helps [specific user] to [core action] so they can [benefit]." If you can fill that in cleanly, you're ready to build. If you can't, you're not — and that's the most valuable thing this module can tell you. Example: "SaleSnap helps market vendors log each sale in two taps so they can see today's real profit."

User flow: the map before the build

Sketch the path a user takes, screen by screen: open app → tap 'new sale' → pick item & price → see profit update → done. This flow becomes your build order and your prompt outline in Module 2. Keep it to the shortest path that delivers value.

🧪 Interactive Lab — Sort features for a vendor sales app
Feature
Log a sale and see today's profit
Save data between sessions
Multi-currency crypto payments
Priority
Core (build first)
Supporting (makes core usable)
Later (‘not yet’ list)

🧪 Blueprint lab (copy → run to spec your app)

You are a product strategist. I want to build an app about [your idea]. Interview me one question at a time to nail down: the ONE specific user, the painful problem it removes, and the single core action that delivers value. Then write my one-sentence app spec in the form “[App] helps [user] to [core action] so they can [benefit],” list the core / supporting / later features, and sketch the shortest user flow screen by screen. Keep it lean — defer everything non-essential.

🔬 Going deeper: validate the problem and write acceptance criteria

Before building, spend one day testing your assumptions. Talk to five real people from your target user group and ask about their past behaviour, not opinions: "How did you track yesterday's sales? What went wrong last week?" If nobody describes the pain unprompted, rethink the problem. Five honest conversations will save you days of building the wrong app.

Next, turn your core action into acceptance criteria — testable statements of what "working" means. A useful format is Given / When / Then: "Given I have logged two sales today, when I log a third sale of 1,500 CFA with cost 900 CFA, then today's profit increases by 600 CFA and the sale appears at the top of the list." Acceptance criteria become your prompts and your tests: if the app passes them, the core works.

Finally, protect your scope with a "not yet" list. Every good idea that is not essential to the core action goes there — reports, multiple users, exports, payments. Scope creep is the main reason first apps never ship. You can always add features after real users ask for them.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Narrow the user brutally. "Everyone" is nobody; one specific user makes every later decision easy.
  • One core action. If you can't name the single most important thing a user does, you're not ready to build.
  • The "not yet" list is your friend. Deferring features is how you actually ship.

📚 Glossary

  • User flow: the screen-by-screen path a user takes to get value.
  • Core action: the single action that delivers the app's main value.
  • App spec: the one-sentence definition of what the app does and for whom.
  • Scope creep: the drift of adding features that delay shipping.

📖 Explore further

  • Level 1's problem-hunting module and Level 2's product module both feed this stage.
  • Marty Cagan, Inspired — on building products people want.

quiz.q: Joseph wants to build 'an app for everyone with a phone to manage their money'. In his Module 1 blueprint, what is the most valuable first revision?

Nothing; a unanimous yes is strong evidence the problem is real

quiz.q: Fill the one-sentence spec for a moto-taxi app: '[RideNet] helps ___ to ___ so they can ___.' Which completion best fits the module's format?
opts: helps the transport sector to digitise its operations so they can be more modern
helps moto-taxi drivers to use AI so they can benefit from new technology
helps Yaoundé moto-taxi drivers log each fare in two taps so they see daily net

quiz.x: A specific user, one core action and a concrete benefit. The last option names the user but its 'action' is using AI, not a task that delivers value.

quiz.q: For a moto-taxi earnings tracker, a learner lists: log a fare, save entries, log fuel spend, share reports with other drivers, and Mobile Money integration. How should 'log fuel spend' be classed?
opts: Not yet: fuel is a nice-to-have that can wait until version two
Core: it is the single action that delivers the app's value to the moto-taxi driver
Core alongside logging fares, since both are financial entries
Supporting: it is needed for the net figure to be correct but is not the core
quiz.x: Fuel spend makes the net correct, so it supports the core fare-logging action. Treating it as co-core is the runner-up but breaks the 'one core action, built first alone' rule.

quiz.q: A Given-When-Then criterion for SaleSnap reads: 'Given a sale of 2,500 CFA with cost 1,800, when I save it, then profit shows ___.' What value makes the test pass?
opts: -700 CFA
+700 CFA
quiz.x: Profit is price minus cost: 2,500 - 1,800 = 700. Subtracting the other way gives -700, the classic sign-error runner-up.

quiz.q: A US nonprofit's app blueprint for volunteer scheduling includes shift sign-up, payroll, inventory, a social feed and AI motivational quotes in version 1. What should the builder do?
opts: Keep shift sign-up as core and move the rest to a 'not yet' list
Drop shift sign-up, as competitors already offer it, and keep the unique features
Cut the social feed but keep payroll and inventory, which are business-critical
Keep all of them but build them in parallel to save time
quiz.x: Scope creep is resolved by one core action plus a 'not yet' list. Keeping payroll and inventory is the runner-up as it sounds serious, but neither serves the volunteer-scheduling problem.

quiz.q: Before building, the module says to talk to how many real users, and asking what kind of question?
opts: One expert user, asking them to design the screens for you
Five users, asking how they handled the problem recently, e.g. yesterday's sales
Twenty users, asking which features they would pay for in a future version of the app
Five users, asking whether they think the app idea is a good one
quiz.x: Five real users, asking about past behaviour. Five users asking for opinions is the runner-up: right number, wrong kind of question.

quiz.q: Grace sketches this user flow for a deposit tracker: open app, pick client, enter deposit, see balance. Why does the module want this sketched before building?
opts: It becomes the build order and the outline for prompts in the next module
It is required by app builders, which refuse to run without a flow diagram
It replaces the need for testing because the flow is already agreed
It lets her design the colour scheme for each screen before features exist
quiz.x: The flow becomes your build order and prompt outline. Colour design is polish, which comes last in the chain, so it is a misplaced use of the flow.

quiz.q: A Kinshasa founder is excited about a voice-controlled AI assistant he has built and is now searching for a problem his gadget could solve. Which maxim from the module challenges this approach?
opts: Ship the small version first and improve it later
One change at a time beats one giant prompt
Fall in love with the problem, not the solution
Charge for the value, not for the effort spent
quiz.x: The problem is what keeps users coming back; the app is just today's answer. 'Ship small' is sound advice but does not address starting from a solution.

quiz.q: A tailor records a 20,000 CFA order with a 5,000 CFA deposit, then a second payment of 6,000 CFA. Under a sound acceptance criterion, what balance should the app show as due?
quiz.x: 20,000 - 5,000 - 6,000 = 9,000. 15,000 is the runner-up: it is the balance after the deposit only, ignoring the second payment.

modules.d: The Team21 method for prompting apps into existence — Foundation, Feature, Refine, Polish.
modules.body:
How to talk an app into existence — in the right order

Throwing one giant prompt at an app builder produces a mess. Operators build in a 4-stage prompt chain, each stage doing one job well. This is the CLEAR framework from Level 1, applied to software: structured, sequential, and reliable. Master this chain and you can build almost anything.

Stage 1 — Foundation (the skeleton)

Establish what you're building and its core structure, before any detail. "Build a mobile-friendly web app called SaleSnap for market vendors. It has one main screen where they log sales. Use a clean, simple design with large tap targets. Set up the basic layout and navigation first." You're pouring the foundation — don't decorate yet.

Stage 2 — Feature (the core action)

Add the one core action from your blueprint. "Now add the core feature: a button to log a new sale. When tapped, let the vendor enter an item name, sale price, and cost. After saving, show today's total sales and profit at the top." One feature, fully working, before the next.

Stage 3 — Refine (make it real & usable)

Add the supporting features and real-world robustness. "Save all sales so they persist when the app is reopened. Add a simple list of today's sales below the total. Handle the case where the vendor leaves a field empty." This is where a toy becomes a tool.

Stage 4 — Polish (the finish)

Improve look, feel, and delight. "Add a dark mode toggle. Make the profit number turn green when positive. Add a small celebration animation on the first sale of the day. Ensure it looks great on a small phone screen." Polish is last — never first.

"Foundation, Feature, Refine, Polish — in that order, every time." Skipping ahead is the #1 cause of tangled, unfixable apps. Build the skeleton before the skin; make it work before you make it beautiful.
The operator's build rules: ① One change at a time — small prompts you can verify beat giant ones you can't. ② Test after every stage — catch problems while they're small. ③ If it works, save it — note the prompt that got you here before the next change. ④ Describe the "what," let AI choose the "how" — say the outcome, not the code.

Prompt
“Build a simple one-screen app with clean layout”
“Add a button to log a sale and show profit”
“Save sales so they persist on reopen”
“Add dark mode and a celebration animation”

2 — Feature
3 — Refine

🧪 Foundation-prompt lab (copy → run in an app builder)

Build a mobile-friendly web app called [name] for [specific user]. Its purpose: [one-sentence spec]. Start with the FOUNDATION only: create one clean main screen with simple navigation and large, easy tap targets. Use a modern, minimal design. Do NOT add features yet — just set up the layout and structure so I can confirm it before we add the core feature.

🔬 Going deeper: anatomy of a strong build prompt

Each stage prompt works best with five parts: context (what the app is and who it serves), the specific change (one thing), details (screens, data fields, behaviours, wording), constraints (mobile-first, large tap targets, keep existing features unchanged) and a test (how you will know it works). Example for Stage 2: "SaleSnap is a mobile app for market vendors. Add a 'New sale' button. Tapping it opens a form with item name, sale price and cost (numbers in CFA). On save, add the sale to today's list and update today's total sales and profit at the top. Do not change the existing layout. After this, I will test by logging a sale of 1,500 with cost 900 and expect profit 600."

Notice the phrase "do not change the existing layout". Builders sometimes rewrite working parts while adding new ones; explicit constraints protect what already works.

Keep a prompt log: each prompt you sent, what happened, and whether it worked. It is your recipe for rebuilding, your rollback map when things break (Module 5), and evidence for your capstone. When a conversation becomes long and confused, start a fresh session and paste in your spec plus the working prompts — a clean context often fixes strange behaviour.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • One change at a time. Small, verifiable prompts are the secret to apps that don't break mysteriously.
  • Never polish early. Animations and dark mode on a broken core is decorating a house with no foundation.
  • Save the working prompt. Before each new change, note what got you here — your prompt chain is your undo button.

📚 Glossary

  • Prompt chain: a sequence of prompts each building on the last.
  • Foundation → Feature → Refine → Polish: the Team21 build order.
  • Persistence: saving data so it survives reopening the app.
  • Tap target: the tappable area of a button — bigger is better on phones.

📖 Explore further

  • Revisit Level 1's CLEAR framework — the prompt chain is CLEAR applied to software.
  • Each app builder has prompting guides; the 4-stage method works across all of them.

modules.t: Rapid App Building: Your First Live App
modules.d: Go hands-on — take a blueprint through the 4-stage chain to a working app you can open right now.
modules.body:
Time to build — for real

You have the paradigm (Module 0), a blueprint (Module 1), and the prompt chain (Module 2). This module is where you produce a working, live app you can open on a screen today. We'll build one together as a worked example — then you build yours. The goal isn't perfection; it's the electric moment of seeing your own idea run.

Worked build: "SaleSnap" from zero to live

  1. Foundation prompt → a clean one-screen app appears. You confirm the layout looks right. Test: does it load and look clean on a phone-sized view?
  2. Feature prompt → the "log a sale" button and profit total appear. Test: can you log a sale and see the total change?
  3. Refine prompt → sales now persist and show in a list; empty fields are handled. Test: reopen — is your data still there?
  4. Polish prompt → dark mode, green profit, a small animation. Test: does it feel good to use?

Four prompts, four tests, one live app. That's the rhythm of every build you'll ever do.

"The first time your own app runs, something changes in you." Every Team21 vibe-coding cohort reports the same thing: the moment an idea in your head becomes a thing on a screen, you stop believing building is for other people. Chase that moment today.

The build rhythm (memorize this)

  • Prompt → Test → Confirm → Next. Never fire the next prompt until the last one works.
  • Preview constantly. App builders show a live preview — keep your eyes on it, not just the chat.
  • When something's off, stop and fix it now — don't pile new features on a broken base (that's Module 4).
  • Commit to shipping the small version. A four-feature app that works beats a twenty-feature app that doesn't exist.
If you get stuck: app builders are conversational — tell it plainly. "The save button isn't working" or "the layout looks broken on mobile" is a perfectly good prompt. Describe what you see vs. what you expected, and let it fix. You don't debug code; you describe symptoms. Module 4 makes you good at this.
🧪 Your build lab (do it now — the whole point of this module)

Using your app builder and your blueprint from Module 1, run the 4-stage chain now: 1) FOUNDATION: “Build a mobile-friendly web app called [name] for [user]; one clean main screen, large tap targets, minimal modern design. Structure only — no features yet.” 2) FEATURE: “Add the core action: [describe your one core action].” 3) REFINE: “Save data so it persists on reopen; add [supporting feature]; handle empty inputs gracefully.” 4) POLISH: “Add [one delight, e.g. dark mode]; make it look great on a small phone.” Test after each stage before moving on.

🧪 Validated exercise

The build rhythm is: Prompt → Test → Confirm → ___.

🔬 Going deeper: think in data, test with edge cases

Every app is built around data. Before your Feature stage, write a simple data model: the things your app stores and their fields. For SaleSnap: Sale — item (text), price (number), cost (number), date and time; profit is calculated (price − cost), not typed. Telling the builder your data model ("store each sale with item, price, cost and timestamp; calculate profit") produces cleaner, more reliable apps than describing screens alone.

Then test like a professional. For each feature, try the happy path (normal use), then edge cases: an empty field, zero, a very large number, a decimal price, text in a number field, two sales in quick succession, closing and reopening the app. Most real-world bugs live in edge cases. Write them down once and reuse them every time you change something — this is called regression testing: making sure new changes did not break old features.

Finally, create save points. Many builders offer version history or checkpoints; after each confirmed step, note the version. If a later change breaks everything, you can return to the last working state in seconds instead of hours.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Keep the preview open. Watch your app change live — it's the fastest feedback loop you'll ever have.
  • Describe symptoms, not solutions. "The total doesn't update" is a great fix prompt; you don't need to know why.
  • Ship the small version. The dopamine of a running app beats the perfectionism of an unbuilt one.

📚 Glossary

  • Live preview: the running app builders show as you build.
  • Build rhythm: prompt → test → confirm → next.
  • Ship: get a working version in front of a real user.

📖 Explore further

  • Pick one builder and do the whole flow once — fluency comes from a complete build, not from reading.
  • Module 4 turns you into a confident debugger when things break.

quiz.x: Fix it now; don't build on a broken base. Restarting is the runner-up because it gives a clean slate, but it throws away everything that already works.

quiz.x: Commit to shipping the small version. Cutting to one feature is defensible minimalism but discards working features users could use now.

quiz.x: The ordered lab starts with the data model, then the prompt. Running regression is good practice, but it comes after changes, not before writing the prompt.

facts.t: Four prompts, four tests, one live app.
facts.more: The SaleSnap worked build: each stage tested before the next — the rhythm of every build.

modules.t: Debugging Without Coding: The Fixer's Mindset
modules.d: When something breaks — and it will — fix it by describing symptoms clearly, not by reading code.
modules.body:
Everything breaks. Fixers stay calm.

The difference between people who succeed at vibe coding and those who quit isn't talent — it's how they react when something breaks. Beginners panic and start over. Fixers treat a bug as a puzzle with a findable answer, and describe it clearly enough for the AI to solve. This module gives you that mindset and a repeatable method, so a broken app is a five-minute detour, not a dead end.

The core reframe: you describe, AI diagnoses

You don't need to read the code to fix the app. Your job is to be a great symptom-reporter — the way you'd describe a car problem to a mechanic. "It makes a grinding noise when I brake" is more useful than a wrong guess about the engine. Same here: describe what you did, what you expected, and what actually happened.

The 4-step debugging method

  1. Reproduce: what exact steps make the problem happen? "When I tap Save with an empty price, nothing happens." Consistency is the first clue.
  2. Describe precisely: tell the AI three things — what you did, what you expected, what actually happened. "I tapped Save; I expected the sale to appear in the list; instead the screen went blank."
  3. Isolate: narrow it down. "It only happens with a decimal price" or "only after I add a second sale." Narrow bugs are easy bugs.
  4. Verify the fix: after the AI changes something, re-test the exact steps. Confirm it's fixed and that nothing else broke.
"A bug is not a verdict on your ability — it's information." Every builder, from beginner to senior engineer, spends much of their time fixing things. The skill isn't avoiding bugs; it's calmly hunting them down. Fixers are made, not born.
Power moves when stuck: ① Ask the AI to explain: "Why might this be happening?" — it often diagnoses itself. ② Ask for options: "Give me three possible causes and how to check each." ③ Roll back: return to the last working version (your saved prompt chain from Module 2) and re-apply changes one at a time. ④ Simplify: "Temporarily remove the animation so we can see if it's causing the freeze."

The mindset rules

  • Don't start over — isolate. Starting from scratch throws away everything that was working.
  • One change at a time when fixing, just like when building — so you know what actually solved it.
  • Stay specific. "It's broken" gets you nowhere; "the total shows NaN after a decimal price" gets you a fix.
  • Keep working versions. Your saved prompt chain is your rollback point — bugs are far less scary when you can always return to "working."
🧪 Interactive Lab — Match the debugging step to the action
Action

“I expected X; instead I got Y”
“It only breaks with a decimal price”

🧪 Debug lab (copy → use whenever something breaks)

Something in my app isn't working. Here's the situation: STEPS TO REPRODUCE: [what I did]. EXPECTED: [what should happen]. ACTUAL: [what actually happened]. It seems to only happen when [any pattern you noticed]. Please give me the three most likely causes, tell me how to confirm which one it is, then fix it — changing one thing at a time — and tell me exactly what to re-test to confirm it's solved.

🔬 Going deeper: the common bug families

Most beginner bugs fall into a few families. Recognising them speeds up diagnosis:

  • Data not saving: information disappears after reopening — persistence was never added or storage is misconfigured.
  • Number problems: "NaN" (not a number), totals wrong, decimals ignored — usually text from an input treated as a number incorrectly, or empty fields.
  • Display not updating: data saves but the screen does not refresh until reload — a state or refresh issue.
  • Layout breaks: buttons off-screen or overlapping on small phones — responsive design problems.
  • Login or permission errors: users cannot sign in or see data — authentication or access-rule problems.
  • Integration errors: payments, email or external services failing — keys, settings or limits.

Two power moves help non-coders. First, many builders and browsers show error messages (sometimes in a console or log). Copy the exact message into your bug report — it is a precise clue. Second, after any fix, run your regression list from Module 4: bugs are often fixed in one place while breaking another.

Remember the honest limit: if a bug involves money, private data or security, and you cannot confidently verify the fix, get help from someone experienced before real users rely on it.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Never start over. Isolate the bug; starting from scratch throws away everything that worked.
  • Ask the AI to diagnose itself. "Why might this be happening?" often solves it in one move.
  • Keep rollback points. Your saved prompt chain means you can always return to a working app.

📚 Glossary

  • Reproduce: reliably trigger the bug on demand.
  • Isolate: narrow a bug to the specific condition that causes it.
  • Rollback: return to a previous working version.
  • Regression: a fix that accidentally breaks something else — always re-test.

📖 Explore further

  • The symptom-reporting habit is the same skill great QA testers use — it transfers everywhere.
  • Module 5's speed challenge will test your fixer reflexes under time pressure.

quiz.q: A Yaoundé user reports: 'A new sale saves, but the list only shows it after I reload.' Which bug family fits best?
opts: Integration settings
Authentication or access rule setup
Data not saving (persistence)
Display not refreshing (state)
quiz.x: The data is saved (it appears after reload) but the screen doesn't update, which is state. Persistence is the runner-up but is ruled out because the reload shows the sale.

quiz.q: Three learners in a Buea cohort each file a bug report about a failing Save button on their sales app. Which report gives the AI the most useful information?
opts: 'The save button sometimes fails, maybe because of the new animation I added yesterday.'
'The app is broken and I think the database is corrupted, please fix it.'
'I tapped Save with price 1,250.50; expected it in the list; got a blank screen.'
'Please rewrite the save function using a more reliable approach.'
quiz.x: Steps, expected and actual. The 'maybe the animation' report is the runner-up as it offers a hypothesis, but it is vague about reproduction.

quiz.q: Blessing's app freezes 'sometimes'. Following the 4-step method, what should she do first?
opts: Roll back to the very first version of the app
Find the exact steps that make it freeze every time
Remove features one by one until it stops freezing
Ask the AI to rewrite the app in a faster, more modern framework
quiz.x: Reproduce first: consistency is the first clue. Removing features is the runner-up (isolation) but comes after you can reliably reproduce the freeze.

quiz.q: A builder in Texas has tried four fixes without success and is considering deleting the project to start over. What does the module recommend instead?
opts: Keep applying fixes, combining several per prompt to save time
Start over; a clean build is usually faster than debugging
Roll back to the last working version and reapply changes one at a time
Hire a developer immediately, since the app is now probably beyond repair
quiz.x: Don't start over: isolate and roll back to your saved working state. Hiring a developer is a reasonable last resort, but premature here.

quiz.q: Mary notices her app only freezes after the celebration animation plays. Which power move best tests that suspicion?
opts: Ask the AI to add a second animation to see if it freezes twice
Ask the AI to rewrite all screens to use a different animation library instead
Ask users to avoid triggering the animation until a new version is ready
Ask the AI to temporarily remove the animation and check if the freeze stops
quiz.x: Simplify: temporarily remove the suspected cause. Swapping the library might work but changes many things at once, so you won't learn what caused the freeze.

quiz.q: Kwame reported that tapping Save with an empty price did nothing, and the AI has just applied a fix. What completes the 4-step method?
opts: Immediately add the next feature to keep momentum
Re-test the exact steps and check nothing else broke
Ask the AI for three other possible causes just in case

modules.d: A timed, graded build — idea to working app in one focused session, proving your fluency.
modules.body:
The plAIbox™ that proves you can build under pressure

Knowledge you can't apply quickly isn't yet a skill. This graded challenge puts a clock on everything you've learned: take a fresh idea from blueprint to working app in one focused session. Speed matters because it proves fluency — and because in the real world, the person who ships this week beats the person still planning next month. This is your vibe-coding black belt test.

The challenge. Pick a simple, real app idea — different from your Module 3 build — and take it through the full pipeline in a single session: blueprint → 4-stage prompt chain → debug → working app. Aim for a genuinely usable core, not a masterpiece. Time-box it; when the clock's up, you ship what you have.

Fast-build ideas (pick one, or bring your own)

  • Tip calculator for your local currency, with bill-splitting.
  • Water / habit tracker with a daily goal and a streak counter.
  • Flashcard app for a subject you're studying.
  • Expense splitter for a group trip or shared household.
  • Simple booking form for a small service business.
  • Countdown / event timer for an upcoming deadline.

The speed-build discipline

  1. Blueprint in 5 minutes. One user, one problem, one core action, one-sentence spec. Don't overthink — pick and go.
  2. Foundation, then Feature. Get the skeleton and the one core action working before anything else. This is your minimum shippable app.
  3. Refine only what's essential. Persistence and empty-input handling — skip the rest under time pressure.
  4. One polish touch. A single delight (dark mode, a color, an icon) — then stop.
  5. Debug calmly. Use the Module 4 method; don't restart, isolate and fix.
"Constraints breed creativity and force shipping." The clock isn't cruelty — it's the thing that turns your careful method into fast instinct. Every timed build makes the next one faster, until building an app feels as natural as writing an email.
Operator truth: your first speed build will feel rushed and imperfect — that's the point. You're training the reflex to ship over the reflex to polish. The imperfect app that exists teaches you more (and can earn more) than the perfect one that never leaves your head.
🧪 Speed-build kickoff (copy → run to blueprint fast)

I'm doing a timed speed-build. My idea: [one line]. In under 2 minutes, give me: the single specific user, the one core action, a one-sentence app spec, and the exact 4 prompts I should fire in sequence (Foundation, Feature, Refine, Polish) to build it fast. Keep each prompt tight and ready to paste into an app builder. Then tell me the ONE thing I should test after each stage.

🧪 Validated exercise

Under time pressure, you train the reflex to ___ over the reflex to polish.

📝 Submission (graded by your mentor)

  • Your working app (a link or recording) plus its one-sentence spec.
  • The 4-stage prompt chain you actually used.
  • One bug you hit and how you fixed it (the fixer's method in action).
  • A one-line reflection: what was faster this time than in Module 3?

🔬 Going deeper: timeboxing and the walking skeleton

Professional teams use timeboxing: fixing the time and flexing the scope. Instead of "build everything, however long it takes", you decide "in 60 minutes, ship whatever works". This forces prioritisation — the core action first, everything else only if time remains.

A useful target is the walking skeleton: the thinnest version of the app that works end to end — open, perform the core action, see the result, data saved. It may look plain, but it walks. Once the skeleton walks, every additional minute improves a working product rather than a broken one.

Plan your timebox before starting: for a 60-minute challenge, roughly 5 minutes blueprint, 10 minutes Foundation, 20 minutes Feature, 15 minutes essential Refine (persistence and empty inputs), 5 minutes one polish touch, 5 minutes deployment and a final test. If you fall behind, cut polish first, then non-essential refinements — never the core action. Keep a short note of where time went; comparing your speed builds over weeks shows your growing fluency.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Pick fast, build faster. The idea matters less than completing the full loop under time.
  • Minimum shippable app first. Foundation + one feature = something real; everything after is bonus.
  • Race your own time. Do this challenge weekly and watch your build speed compound.

📚 Glossary

  • Time-box: a fixed time limit that forces completion.
  • Minimum shippable app: foundation + the single core feature working.
  • Speed build: a full idea-to-app pipeline in one focused session.

📖 Explore further

  • Repeat with a new idea weekly — fluency is built by finishing, not by reading.
  • Module 6 turns these apps into income.

modules.t: Monetization: Turn Your App Into Income
modules.d: From working app to paying users — pricing models, payment setup, and your first real revenue.
modules.body:
An app that helps people can be an app that pays you

You can now build working apps. This module turns that capability into income. The good news: you already learned the business fundamentals in Level 1 (problem, validation, WHY) and Level 2 (digital products, value-based pricing). Here you apply them specifically to apps — how to charge, how to take payment, and how to get your first paying user. Building is the skill; monetizing is the reward.

The main ways apps make money

  • One-time purchase: users pay once to buy or unlock the app. Simplest to start; best for tools with lasting value.
  • Subscription: a recurring fee for ongoing value or updates. Best for apps used repeatedly — predictable income, but you must keep delivering.
  • Freemium: a free core with paid premium features. Great for growth — many users try free, some convert. The most common model for a reason.
  • Client work: build a custom app for a business that pays you directly — often the fastest first income (ties to Level 2 freelancing).
  • Ads / sponsorship: only worthwhile at real scale; ignore it early.
"Charge for the value, not the effort." An app that saves a small business ten hours a month is worth far more than the weekend it took you to build — the same value-based pricing you learned as an operator, now applied to software.

Getting to your first paying user

  1. Solve a real, painful problem for a specific someone — the same blueprint discipline from Module 1. People pay to remove pain, not to admire features.
  2. Price with confidence. Too cheap signals low value; base the price on what the problem is worth to the user.
  3. Set up payment for your market. Internationally, app stores, Stripe, Gumroad, or Paddle; locally, mobile money and direct arrangements. Meet users where they already pay — friction kills sales.
  4. Sell to an audience you can reach. Your community, your WhatsApp list, a specific business — your first ten users come from people you can actually contact, not strangers.
  5. Client-first is a shortcut. Building one custom app for one paying business gets you revenue this month while you grow a product on the side.
Regional operator note: in many markets the fastest path isn't an app-store product — it's building a simple, genuinely useful tool for a local business (a booking app for a clinic, a stock tracker for a shop) and charging a setup fee plus a small monthly amount, paid by mobile money. Real problems + local payment rails = real income, no app store required.

A daily-use tool with ongoing updates

A custom booking app for one clinic

🧪 Monetization lab (copy → run on your app)

You are a product-monetization strategist. My app: [describe it and its user]. Recommend the best revenue model (one-time, subscription, freemium, or client work) and why. Suggest a specific price anchored to the value it delivers, the right payment setup for [my market], and the single fastest way to land my first paying user from an audience I can already reach. Then give me a short, honest sales message I could send to that first prospect today.

🔬 Going deeper: price with numbers, sell with trust

Value-based pricing becomes concrete with simple arithmetic. If your stock-tracking app saves a shop owner 8 hours a month and their time is worth about 1,500 CFA per hour, it creates roughly 12,000 CFA of value monthly; reducing stock losses of 20,000 CFA adds more. A price of 5,000 CFA per month is easy to justify. Present the value, not your effort.

Check your unit economics: monthly revenue per customer minus the costs of serving them (builder subscription share, hosting, payment fees, your support time). If each client pays 5,000 CFA, mobile money fees are around 2%, and your hosting and tools cost 15,000 CFA per month in total, you need at least four clients just to cover costs — plan your first sales target accordingly.

Earn trust as a software provider. Write a simple agreement for client work (what you deliver, price, payment schedule, support period, what happens to data). If your app stores customers' personal information, tell them what you collect and why, protect it, and respect data protection rules in your country. Small businesses buy from people they trust — reliability and honesty are your strongest sales tools.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Client-first for fast cash. One custom app for one paying business beats waiting for app-store downloads.
  • Don't underprice. Too cheap signals low value; price on the problem's worth to the user.
  • Match payment to your market. Mobile money and direct arrangements often beat app stores locally.

📚 Glossary

  • Freemium: free core, paid premium features.
  • Subscription: recurring fee for ongoing value.
  • Value-based pricing: price set by value delivered, not effort spent.
  • Payment rail: the method money moves (app store, Stripe, mobile money).

📖 Explore further

  • Level 2's income modules (digital products & freelancing) apply directly here.
  • Payment tools (verify availability in your market): Stripe, Paddle, Gumroad, local mobile money.

modules.t: Ship It: Your App on Real Phones
modules.d: Deploy, get a shareable link, put it on real devices, and complete the capstone — idea to income.
modules.body:
The last mile: from your screen to the world's phones

An app that only runs in your builder's preview isn't shipped. This final module gets your app deployed to a real, shareable link that works on real phones — and completes your vibe-coding capstone. Shipping is the whole point: it's the difference between "I'm learning to build apps" and "I built an app you can use right now." This is where you cross that line.

How modern deployment works (the easy path)

  • One-click publish: most AI app builders deploy your app to a live URL with a single button. No servers, no configuration — you get a link you can share instantly.
  • It's a web app first: your app runs in any phone's browser via that link. This works everywhere, on any device, with no app-store approval — ideal for reaching users fast, especially in mobile-first markets.
  • "Add to Home Screen": users can save your web app to their phone's home screen, where it behaves almost like a native app — icon and all. Teach your users this one trick.
  • App stores come later. Google Play / the App Store are for when you have traction and a reason. Don't let store complexity delay your launch — ship the web app now.
"Real artists ship." — Steve Jobs. The world is full of brilliant ideas that never left someone's head. The entire value of everything you learned in this course is unlocked by one act: putting a working link in a real person's hands.

Your pre-launch checklist

  • Works on a real phone — test on an actual device, not just the preview. Screens are smaller; thumbs are bigger.
  • The core action works flawlessly — everything else can be rough, but the one thing that delivers value must be solid.
  • Data persists — users' information survives closing and reopening.
  • A clear first step — a new user knows what to do within five seconds of opening it.
  • Your name/contact on it — so users can reach you (and so it's yours).
🎓 The Vibe Coding capstone. Ship a real, working app, deployed to a live link, that solves a genuine problem for a real user — built through the 4-stage prompt chain, with your prompt log and one documented bug-fix. Bonus: a monetization plan from Module 6 and evidence of your first user. Passing every module (75%+) plus this capstone earns the Vibe Coding Mastery certificate — a print-ready PDF with a QR validation code, signed by Innocent Forteh, Program Director, Team21 Academy.
You are now a builder. Six modules ago, "I can't code" may have felt like a wall. You've just taken an idea to a live app on a real phone. That capability — turning thought into working software by describing it clearly — puts you among a small and rapidly-valued group. The Architect's path (deeper frameworks, agentic apps) is open whenever you want it.
🧪 Ship-it lab (copy → run to launch)

Help me ship my app. It's built and working in my app builder. Walk me through: (1) deploying it to a live shareable link, (2) a final pre-launch checklist to test on a real phone, (3) how to tell users to “Add to Home Screen” so it feels native, and (4) a short, friendly launch message I can send to my first users with the link. Then give me one clear next step to get my very first real user this week.

🧪 Validated exercise

🔬 Going deeper: security and privacy before you share the link

Shipping fast must not mean shipping carelessly. In 2025, security researchers reported that many apps built with AI app builders exposed users' data because database access rules were not configured — anyone who found the app's address could read or change other people's records. The apps "worked"; they were simply unsafe.

Before launching an app that stores other people's data, check: ① Authentication — users must sign in before seeing private data. ② Access rules — each user can only read and change their own records (on platforms such as Supabase this is configured with row-level security; ask your builder to enable and explain it). ③ No secrets in the front end — API keys for payments or AI services belong on the server side or in the platform's secret settings. ④ Test as an outsider — create a second account and confirm it cannot see the first account's data. ⑤ Minimise data — collect only what you need.

After launch, add simple analytics (how many people open the app and complete the core action) and a feedback channel (a WhatsApp link or form). Watch three real users try the app, fix what confuses them, release an improved version, and repeat. Shipping is not the end; it is the start of learning from reality.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Ship the web app now. Don't let app-store complexity delay reaching real users — a link works everywhere today.
  • Teach ‘Add to Home Screen.’ It makes your web app feel native and keeps users coming back.
  • Test on a real phone. Thumbs and small screens reveal what the preview hides.

📚 Glossary

  • Deploy: publish your app to a live, shareable URL.
  • Web app: an app that runs in a browser via a link, on any device.
  • Add to Home Screen: saving a web app so it behaves like a native app.
  • Capstone: the shipped, real app that completes the course.

quiz.q: A Bafoussam builder tested her membership app only in the builder preview on her laptop. What does the pre-launch checklist require next?

Publish to the Google Play Store so the app gets an official quality review first

Test on an actual phone, since small screens and thumbs reveal hidden issues
quiz.x: Test on a real device. Shrinking the browser window is the runner-up: it simulates width but not touch, thumbs or real performance.

quiz.q: Why does the module recommend shipping a web app link first rather than going straight to app stores?
opts: It runs on any device with no store approval, reaching users fast
App stores currently refuse to list apps that were built with AI tools
Web apps cannot be copied by competitors
Web apps are inherently more secure than app-store apps
quiz.x: A web link works everywhere with no approval; stores come later with traction. The store-ban claim is false and the security claim overstates it.

quiz.q: A youth-club app's database access rules were left at the default. What risk does the module highlight?
opts: Anyone with the address might read or change records
Users will be unable to add the app to the home screen
The app may load slowly on older phones
The app will be rejected by the builder platform
quiz.x: Unconfigured rules can expose records. Broken access control topped the OWASP Top 10 (2021). Slow loading is a real issue but unrelated to access rules.

quiz.q: A builder in Abidjan signs in with a second test account and can see account A's records. What does this mean?
opts: The app is ready to launch, since sign-in works correctly
Ready to launch provided the shared data contains no payment details at all
A display bug that will fix itself after deployment
Not ready to launch: access control is broken, however well it 'works'
quiz.x: If account B can see A's data, you're not ready. The 'no payment details' option is the runner-up, but personal data still needs protection.

quiz.q: Which security practice keeps each user seeing only their own rows on platforms like Supabase?
opts: Hiding the data table from the app's navigation menu
Row-level security, which must be enabled and configured
A longer admin password stored in the front-end code of the app
Turning on dark mode for the admin dashboard
quiz.x: Row-level security (RLS) restricts rows per user. Hiding the table from navigation is the runner-up but is cosmetic; the data stays reachable.

quiz.q: A membership app collects name, phone, date of birth and home address 'just in case'. What does the module advise?
opts: Keep the address but store it in a separate table
Keep everything but ask users to agree to terms
Collect only what you need; drop the home address
Keep all fields, since more data allows better features later
quiz.x: Minimise data: collect only what you need. Consent terms are the runner-up, but they don't justify collecting unneeded data.

quiz.q: Order the launch sequence: (a) deploy to a live link, (b) run security checks and outsider test, (c) test the core action on a real phone, (d) send the link with home-screen instructions.
opts: c, a, b, d
b, c, a, d
a, then b, c, d
b, a, c, d
quiz.x: Secure, test, ship, learn. Testing after deploying (b, a, c, d) is the runner-up, but the module tests on a phone before shipping.

quiz.q: A Philadelphia learner shipped her app and wants to know what to do next. What does the module suggest?
opts: Rebuild it as a native app before talking to any users
Stop development, since shipping is the end of the project
Wait for 1,000 users before making any changes
Watch three real people use it, fix, release, repeat
quiz.x: Shipping starts learning from reality. Waiting for 1,000 users is the runner-up but delays the feedback three users give you.

quiz.q: A Nairobi learner asks what she must do to earn the Vibe Coding Mastery certificate at the end of this course. What does the module say?
opts: Passing every module at 75%+ plus the capstone app on a live link
Publishing an app on Google Play with at least 100 downloads
Passing the final module at 90% and submitting a monetisation plan
Completing the speed build in under 30 minutes
quiz.x: Every module at 75%+ plus the capstone. The monetisation plan is a bonus, which is why the second option is the tempting runner-up.

quiz.q: A new user opens your app. The checklist says they should know what to do within how long?
opts: After a short tutorial video
About one minute
About five seconds
About thirty seconds
quiz.x: A clear first step within five seconds. A tutorial video is the runner-up for onboarding, but the module wants the screen itself to be obvious.

facts.more: Users reading or changing data they shouldn't is the most common serious web-app weakness — exactly the risk in unconfigured AI-built apps.

facts.t: Watch three real people use it, fix, release, repeat.
